title: Only comfort
hookLine: the Heidelberg Catechism begins: what is your only comfort in life and death?

cards: What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the very first question of a catechism, a book of questions and answers for teaching the faith. It doesn't open with the nature of God or the order of the universe.

It opens with the question someone asks at a sickbed, or lying awake in the small hours. The book is the Heidelberg Catechism, named for the German city it came from, and still taught in some Reformed churches.
Some learn its first answer by heart and carry it for life.

teach.b: Here's the answer, put plainly. That I am not my own. That I belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ.

It goes on: he has paid for my sins and set me free; he watches over me so that not a hair can fall from my head without the Father's will; and by his Spirit he makes me willing and ready to live for him.

teach.h: COMFORT IS BELONGING, NOT A MOOD.
teach.b: Comfort here isn't a mood that comes and goes. It's a fact about belonging: whose you are. It starts with a negative, not my own, close to Paul's words: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price."
To some ears that sounds like a loss. The catechism hears it as relief. If I am not my own, I don't have to hold myself together.

teach.h: WHETHER WE LIVE OR DIE, THE LORD'S.
teach.b: And to the Romans: "whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's." The hairs of your head echo Jesus in Matthew: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered."

The second question asks what you need to know to live and die in this comfort, and answers in three parts: how great my sin and misery are, how I am set free from them, and how I am to thank God for that freedom.

Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it, and the rest of the catechism follows that order. Other churches have their own catechisms; Luther wrote a small one too, back on day eight hundred fifty-eight.
Heidelberg chose to begin with comfort.

how: In Reformed churches that use the Heidelberg Catechism, it is taught to young people and new members, and some congregations preach through it in sections called Lord's Days over the course of a year.

games.why: Heidelberg begins with comfort: the bedside question before the classroom one. its answer: I am not my own, but belong to my faithful Savior.

practice: Ask yourself honestly: what is my comfort, in life and in death? Don't hurry to a right answer; notice what comes up first, a person, a place, a habit, a hope, a blank, and let it be.
If you pray, set the catechism's line, I am not my own, beside whatever came up and see how they sit together; if not, stay with the question.
